title: AQA GCSE Physics · Magnetism and the Motor Effect

items.stem: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of a second bar magnet. What happens to the magnets?

options.text: They repel each other, because the two poles are alike
They attract, because magnets always pull each other
Nothing happens until the two magnets are touching
They repel only if one of the magnets is stronger

items.why: Two like poles repel each other, so two north poles push apart.

items.stem: Two magnets on a bench push each other apart while there is still a 2 cm gap between them. Which statement best describes this force?

options.text: It is a contact force passed through the bench surface
It is a non-contact force, acting across the air gap
It is a non-contact force only while they move
It is a contact force acting through the air

items.why: Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force, so the force acts over a distance.

items.stem: A steel paper clip is held near a strong magnet and becomes magnetic itself. What name is given to the paper clip while it is in the field?

options.text: The clip is a permanent magnet
The clip is a non-magnetic metal
The clip is an induced magnet
The clip is a magnetic pole

items.why: An induced magnet is a material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field.

items.stem: A chain of paper clips hangs from a bar magnet. The magnet is taken away. What happens to the paper clips?

options.text: They stay in a chain, now permanently magnetic
They push each other apart and scatter widely
They stay in a chain for the next few hours
They lose their magnetism and fall apart

items.why: When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.

items.stem: The south pole of one bar magnet is brought near the north pole of another. Which row correctly describes the force?

options.text: Repulsion, because these two poles are different
Attraction, because unlike poles attract each other
Attraction, because south poles always attract
No force at all, as the poles are not alike

items.why: Two unlike poles attract each other, and this happens for any pair of N and S poles.

items.stem: A student wants two magnets on trolleys to push apart when released. How should the magnets be arranged?

options.text: With a north pole facing a south pole
With the two magnets touching end to end
With two north poles facing each other
With one magnet turned on its side

items.why: Two like poles repel each other, so N facing N gives a push apart.

items.stem: Which statement gives a correct difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?

options.text: An induced magnet keeps its magnetism when it is removed
A permanent magnet can only ever attract things
An induced magnet has a fixed north pole and south pole
A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field

items.why: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field, while an induced magnet only becomes magnetic in a field.

items.stem: An iron nail is brought near the south pole of a magnet and is pulled in. The magnet is then turned round so the north pole faces the nail. What happens?

options.text: The nail is still pulled towards the magnet
The nail is pushed away, as the pole has changed
The nail is pushed away only when it is close
The nail now feels no force from this new pole

items.why: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction, whichever pole faces it.

items.stem: Which of these is the best definition of a magnetic field?

options.text: The set of lines drawn on a diagram around a bar magnet
The area a magnet covers when it is touching an object
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet
The space that fills with force once iron is placed in it

items.why: The magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.

items.stem: A magnet is held over a tray containing a copper coin, a nickel disc, an aluminium strip and a steel screw. Which objects are attracted?

options.text: All four of them, since they are all metals
The copper coin and the steel screw
Only the steel screw and nothing else
Only the nickel disc and the steel screw

items.why: Nickel and steel are magnetic materials; copper and aluminium are not.

items.stem: A bar magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron bar. The magnet is then flipped end for end. Which statement about the force on the iron bar is correct?

options.text: It stays an attraction, whichever pole faces the bar
It now changes from an attraction to a strong repulsion
It becomes zero, because the two poles now cancel out
It stays a repulsion for each of the two poles

items.why: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.

items.stem: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?

options.text: In the middle of the magnet
At the poles of the magnet
Equally strong at every point
At the outer ends of the lines

items.why: The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.

items.stem: A plotting compass is moved slowly away from the north pole of a bar magnet. What happens to the magnetic field where the compass is?

options.text: It stays exactly the same until a definite edge is reached
It gets stronger as the compass moves away from the pole
It stays the same all the way around the bar magnet
It gets weaker, because the distance from the magnet increases

items.why: The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet, so moving away weakens it.

items.stem: Outside a bar magnet, which way do the magnetic field lines point?

options.text: From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole across to the north
From each pole in towards the middle
Always straight out from each pole

items.why: The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole.

items.stem: A compass is placed at a point in the field of a bar magnet. What does the direction the needle's north end points in tell you?

options.text: The straight line from that point to the nearest pole
The direction of the magnetic field at that point
The direction the compass would travel if released
The way that a south pole would be pushed there

items.why: The direction of the field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.

items.stem: What is inside a magnetic compass?

options.text: A light piece of iron
A coil of thin wire
A small bar magnet
A drop of liquid metal

items.why: A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet, free to turn.

items.stem: A compass is placed on a bench with no magnets anywhere near it. What does the needle do?

options.text: It settles pointing along the Earth's own magnetic field
It keeps spinning slowly, as there is no field present
It points towards the coldest part of the whole room
It points straight downwards towards the floor

items.why: The Earth has a magnetic field, and the compass needle points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.

items.stem: A student is plotting the field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Which method is correct?

options.text: Slide the compass all the way round the magnet while touching it
Mark a dot at each end of the needle, then move the compass on
Draw a straight line from the compass to the nearest pole
Put the compass down and draw round the outside of it

items.why: Marking both ends and moving the compass so its tail sits on the last head dot builds up one field line, which is then joined and given an arrow.

items.stem: A student draws the field pattern of a bar magnet. Which feature of the drawing shows that the field is stronger near the poles?

options.text: The lines are drawn a long way apart there
The lines are drawn with two arrows on them
The lines are drawn closer together there
The lines are drawn longer at the poles

items.why: Lines drawn closer together represent a stronger field, and they are most crowded at the poles.

items.stem: A compass points the same way on a bench, in a field and out at sea, with no magnets nearby. What does this suggest about the Earth?

options.text: The ice at the North Pole acts like a magnet
The atmosphere is what pulls the needle
The Earth's gravity is turning the needle
The core of the Earth must be magnetic

items.why: A field present everywhere with no magnet nearby must be produced by the Earth itself, which is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

items.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a steady current. What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around the wire?

options.text: Circles centred on the wire and lying in a plane at right angles to it
Straight lines that spread out from the wire, like spokes on a wheel
Straight lines running parallel to the wire along its whole length
Loops that leave one end of the wire and enter at the other end

items.why: The field around a straight current-carrying wire is a set of concentric circles perpendicular to it.

items.stem: A plotting compass is moved from 2 cm to 6 cm away from a wire carrying a steady current. The current is not changed. What happens to the deflection of the compass?

options.text: It stays the same, because the current through the wire is unchanged
It falls to zero, because the field stops at the outer circle
It gets smaller, because the field is weaker further from the wire
It gets larger, because the field circles are wider further out

items.why: Field strength depends on distance from the wire as well as on the current, so it falls as the compass is moved away.

items.stem: A student winds a straight wire into a solenoid and passes the same current through it as before. What happens to the magnetic field produced?

options.text: It is weaker, because the current now has a longer path to run
It is stronger, because the fields of the turns add together
It is unchanged, because the current in the wire is unchanged
There is no field at all until an iron core is in the coil

items.why: Shaping a wire into a solenoid increases the strength of the field, because each turn adds its field to its neighbours'.

items.stem: What best describes the magnetic field inside a long solenoid that is carrying a current?

options.text: Strong at the very centre of the coil and almost zero elsewhere
A set of circles running round the axis, as around a straight wire
Weak inside the coil and strongest just outside the windings
Strong and uniform, drawn as evenly spaced parallel lines

items.why: The specification states that the field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform, so the lines are parallel and evenly spaced.

items.stem: How does the magnetic field around the outside of a current-carrying solenoid compare with that of a bar magnet?

options.text: It is a set of circles around the middle of the coil, not like a bar magnet
It has a similar shape, with one end acting as a north pole and one as a south
It has exactly the same shape, but the ends of a solenoid are not poles
There is no field outside the coil, so no comparison can be made

items.why: The specification states that the field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet.

items.stem: An iron core is placed inside a solenoid that is carrying a current. What is the effect?

options.text: The solenoid begins to produce a magnetic field for the first time
The field grows stronger and stays on after the current is off
The core carries a current of its own that adds to the field
The magnetic field of the solenoid becomes considerably stronger

items.why: Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid; the arrangement is an electromagnet.

items.stem: Which observation best demonstrates that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field?

options.text: A compass beside the wire swings round when the current is switched on
A plotting compass beside the wire keeps pointing north when the current is off
The wire becomes noticeably warmer when the current is switched on
A piece of copper wire placed beside the wire is pulled sideways towards it

items.why: The compass responds only to a magnetic field, and it moves exactly when the current begins, so the current is the cause.

items.stem: The direction of the current in a straight wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field pattern?

options.text: The pattern and the arrows on it are both completely unchanged
The circles turn into straight lines pointing back along the wire
The circles stay, but the arrows point the other way round
The circles are replaced by a bar-magnet pattern with swapped poles

items.why: The pattern is fixed by the shape of the wire and the direction by the direction of the current, so only the arrows reverse.

items.stem: A student is asked to draw the magnetic field of a current-carrying solenoid, showing its direction. Which drawing is correct?

options.text: Parallel lines inside the coil and loops outside it, with no arrows on any line
Parallel arrows inside the coil that start at one end and stop at the other
Closely spaced parallel arrows inside the coil, looping outside from north to south
Circles drawn around the outside of the coil, with clockwise arrows shown

items.why: Inside the coil the field is uniform and along the axis; outside, each line loops back, giving the bar-magnet shape.

items.stem: Why does winding a wire into a solenoid increase the magnetic effect of the current?

options.text: The field of each turn points the same way inside the coil, so they add up
Winding the wire into a coil increases the current flowing in it
The coiled wire has a much larger resistance, and that strengthens the field
The turns of wire trap the field lines so that none can escape the coil

items.why: Many turns contribute their fields at the same place and in the same direction, so the total field is much stronger.

items.stem: A relay diagram shows a coil wound on an iron core in one circuit, and a pivoted iron armature that closes contacts in a second circuit. How does the relay work?

options.text: The current in the coil flows on through the contacts and into the second circuit
The magnetised iron core repels the armature and pushes it onto the contacts
The coil heats the armature, which bends until it touches the contacts
A small current magnetises the core, so the armature closes the contacts

items.why: The coil's magnetic effect moves the armature, so a small current in one circuit switches on a separate circuit.

items.stem: A wire carrying a current is held at right angles to the field between the poles of a magnet. Which statement about the forces is correct?

options.text: Only the wire feels a force, as the magnet carries no current
The magnet and the wire each exert a force on the other
Only the magnet feels a force, because it produces the field
Neither feels a force until the wire is free to move about

items.why: The specification states that the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other.

items.stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what do the first finger, the second finger and the thumb represent?

options.text: The first finger is the current, the second the field, the thumb the motion
The first finger is the force, the second the field, and the thumb current
The right hand is used, with the field, current and force in that order
The first finger the field, the second finger the current, and the thumb the force

items.why: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion: the three are held at right angles to one another.

items.stem: A horizontal wire carries a current from left to right. The magnetic field between the poles is directed into the page. In which direction is the force on the wire?

options.text: Downwards, at right angles to both the field and the current
Upwards, at right angles to both the current and the field
Into the page, in the same direction as the field itself
To the right, in the same direction as the current

items.why: First finger into the page and second finger to the right puts the thumb, and so the force, upwards.

items.stem: Which change would increase the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?

options.text: Using much longer connecting leads between the cell and the wire
Using a much longer wire, most of it outside the field
Using a stronger magnet, so that the flux density is larger
Reducing the current so that less energy is lost as heat

items.why: The force depends on the magnetic flux density, the current and the length of conductor in the field.

items.stem: A straight wire carrying a current is placed so that it lies along the magnetic field lines. What is the force on the wire?

options.text: Zero, because the wire is not at right angles to the field
The largest possible force, as the wire lies along the field
Exactly the same force as when the wire is at right angles to it
A force along the wire, in the direction of the current in it

items.why: The equation applies to a conductor at right angles to the field; a wire lying along the field feels no force.

items.stem: For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current, which word equation gives the force on the conductor?

options.text: force = magnetic field strength × current × length
force = magnetic flux density × charge × length
force = magnetic flux density × current × length
force = magnetic flux density × current × time

items.why: This is the equation as the specification states it, for a conductor at right angles to the field.

items.stem: In the equation F = B I l, what do the symbols B and l stand for?

options.text: B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of conductor in the field
B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of the whole circuit
B is the number of field lines drawn and l is the length of the wire
B is the force from the magnet and l is the length of the conductor

items.why: B is the flux density in tesla and l is the length of the conductor that lies inside the field, in metres.

items.stem: Which set of units should be used when the equation F = B I l is applied?

options.text: F in newtons, B in newtons, I in amperes and l in metres
F in newtons, B in tesla, I in volts and l in centimetres
F in joules, B in tesla, I in amperes and l in metres
F in newtons, B in tesla, I in amperes and l in metres

items.why: These are the units given in the specification: force in newtons, flux density in tesla, current in amperes, length in metres.

items.stem: A wire of length 0.30 m lies at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. The current in the wire is 2.0 A. What is the force on the wire?
items.why: F = B I l = 0.20 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.12 N, with the length already in metres.

items.stem: A wire of length 0.30 m carries a current of 8.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field. The force on the wire is 4.8 N. What is the magnetic flux density?
items.why: Rearranging gives B = F ÷ (I × l) = 4.8 ÷ (8.0 × 0.30) = 2.0 T.

items.stem: A rectangular coil carrying a current is mounted on an axle between the poles of a magnet. Why does the coil tend to rotate?

options.text: The forces on both of its sides act in the same direction, pushing it
The coil becomes a magnet and is pulled towards the north pole
The forces on its opposite sides act in opposite directions
The current warms the coil, which expands and turns on its axle

items.why: The current runs opposite ways along the two sides, so the forces on them are opposite and turn the coil.

items.stem: In a simple d.c. motor, what is the job of the split-ring commutator?

options.text: It carries the current into the coil, so that a force can act on the coil
It reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so it keeps turning one way
It reverses the magnetic field every half turn, so the coil keeps going
It holds the coil steady so that it turns at a constant rate of spin

items.why: Swapping the connections as the coil passes the vertical swaps the two forces over and keeps the rotation going.

items.stem: How does a moving-coil loudspeaker produce sound?

options.text: Pressure variations in the air move the cone, which produces a current
The permanent magnet vibrates and passes its vibrations to the cone
The current heats the coil, and the expanding air makes the sound
A varying current in the coil makes it move and push the cone

items.why: The motor effect gives the current-carrying coil a varying force, so the coil and the cone attached to it move in and out.

items.stem: Loudspeakers and headphones use the motor effect. Which conversion do they carry out?

options.text: Pressure variations in a sound wave into variations in current
Movement of a coil in a magnetic field into an induced current in it
Variations in current into a steady push on the air in the room
Variations in current in a circuit into pressure variations in a sound wave

items.why: The specification states that they convert variations in current in electrical circuits to pressure variations in sound waves.
